# SYCL graph host-task feasibility for segmented decode (round 271)

## Finding

A SYCL graph with a host-task at the existing completed-segment / CPU-callback boundary is a plausible way to express the current segmented verifier protocol declaratively. It can move the host/device ownership transition into a graph dependency: the predecessor graph work completes, then the host-task reads the route/control data and performs the CPU callback, then dependent graph work runs. That preserves the essential safety rule: host code does not inspect device-written mapped control state while device work is in flight. It does **not** establish a way to remove the cost of a host rendezvous. Intel's DPC++ graph design explicitly partitions a graph around host-task nodes and synchronizes partitions in the runtime. So this should be evaluated as a replacement for application-issued per-layer `stream_sync` + graph launch, not assumed to erase the corresponding device/host/device boundary. A runtime may submit predecessor partition, wait, run host task, then submit successor partition on every replay.

The SYCL graph specification says host tasks are valid graph nodes, but may prevent submission of the whole executable graph to the device at once; native-recording mode has a separate host-task API/constraint. The local Intel graph implementation design says host-task nodes trigger graph partitioning, with predecessors, host task, and successors placed in separate partitions, and runtime-managed synchronization between partitions. This is the central cost/safety tradeoff. Sources: Intel graph extension, `sycl_ext_oneapi_graph.asciidoc` lines 2186–2213; Intel graph implementation design, `CommandGraph.md` lines 140–164; usage guide lines 45–67. The upstream primary docs are also published at [SYCL Graph Extension](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/sycl/sycl/doc/extensions/experimental/sycl_ext_oneapi_graph.asciidoc), [Command-Graph Extension design](https://intel.github.io/llvm/design/CommandGraph.html), and [SYCL Graph Usage Guide](https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/sycl/sycl/doc/syclgraph/SYCLGraphUsageGuide.md).

## Evidence and limits

Closed Main receipt `/home/yayoi/.local/state/strata-sycl/post-reboot-tuning-20261007/main-decode-criticalpath-model-root-v1/xe-timed1-on/record.json`, SHA-256 `de826d6cd915b121801ebb3ba5d5f86f0945d82ae6f0819a59bc974c094b71dc`, records an inactive, complete, passed, normal-QUIT run: 32,768 input tokens, 16 output tokens, `performance_eligible=false`, `full_context_runtime_qualified=false`. It used `G16`, cache 128, pool-workers 5, spec 4, prefill 8192, context 262144. Its 16-window decode diagnostic is 124.09 ms/window, decomposed as verify 121.44 (GPU-reach wait 50.27 + per-layer host 55.16 [plan .05, actq .07, jobs .04, CPU 50.64] + stage .49) plus commit/emit 2.65. This is one diagnostic sample, not a qualified speed result. It identifies the host callback/service interval as a substantial measurement target; it does not prove CPU arithmetic itself dominates, nor that SYCL graph partition overhead will be lower.

The integrated source revision examined is WN `0691bcdf5af63a85b3b25650f367d3276db64035`. In `src/core/verify.cpp:415–421`, segmented mode is selected whenever `host_handoff_concurrent` is false, absent explicit override. `verify.cpp:1514–1619` launches the first segment, synchronizes the compute stream before reading mapped sequence/input data and invoking host work, synchronizes the copy stream before publishing completion flags, and launches the next segment. Final drain/error handling is at `1447–1460` and `1612–1620`. In `src/core/expert_source.cpp:1733–1751`, `fetch_dma` enqueues route-data copies on the copy queue and `launch_host` publishes its host handoff; hit work can be enqueued on the compute stream at `1900–1980`. Preserve both queue dependencies, the copy-drain/error path, fences, sequence/route ownership, and the single-owner host handoff. Do not replace these with polling or simultaneous volatile reads.

The Intel documentation/spec text gives no guarantee that a host-task graph is faster than these explicit cuts. In fact, `CommandGraph.md:142–164` describes runtime-managed synchronization between graph partitions and a partition on each side of the host task. It also notes command-buffer support is backend-dependent and reported through graph aspects (`:35–50`). The available local Intel LLVM source snapshot declares SYCL 9.0.0 in `sycl/CMakeLists.txt:105–113`; it is not the deployed Strata SYCL 7.1.1 runtime and cannot establish behavior for that runtime or the B570 combination. The official runtime's exact version, graph aspect support, host-task replay behavior, and graph update behavior must be checked in the actual build/receipt before treating the path as available. No runtime, hardware, build, or performance test was run for this audit.

Local source fingerprints (read-only files):

- `sycl/doc/extensions/experimental/sycl_ext_oneapi_graph.asciidoc`: `0b3b170d9b60c504ecc9010a244d20efe3641b962e2dabee67d3d95f9094656d`
- `sycl/doc/syclgraph/SYCLGraphUsageGuide.md`: `fc8e247406b813002b35dc6e7f6557d3b1926849596784a3a9ff57e63e2de05b`
- `sycl/doc/design/CommandGraph.md`: `11c1a0fa09f96ba3cf8783b747dc7ca40a67c36c21607f6bfda8c185282c97b1`.
- `sycl/CMakeLists.txt` declares 9.0.0 (`SYCL_MAJOR_VERSION 9`, `MINOR 0`, `PATCH 0` at lines 105–113); this snapshot is architecture evidence only, not a 7.1.1 conformance claim.
- Runtime source inspected: `sycl/source/detail/scheduler/scheduler.cpp:510–540` (`ba4a7902712fcfad49f18e11bd4e2bd6b460dde0b86a89130d30976c2f0ff282`) marks a host-task event complete and enqueues its now-unblocked dependent commands; `sycl/source/detail/scheduler/graph_builder.cpp:1205–1272` (`9e53184ba65e703e12a9f24c1d53ecb47a88db674ea1168d40921c2d6daf56e3`) creates a host-task command when connecting events across contexts. These show dependency scheduling mechanics, not backend graph replay latency.

## Minimal architecture worth qualifying

Prototype one opt-in segmented verifier backend using an explicit graph with three ordered regions per host decision: (1) existing device pre-segment; (2) one host-task that waits by graph dependency, consumes only the now-completed handoff slot, runs the same CPU routing/dispatch callback, and writes the next slot; (3) existing device post-segment dependent on that task. Use one stable, preallocated host-visible descriptor slot per serialized request, and do not mutate/reuse it until the graph execution and required queue work have drained. The graph successor may consume host-written data only after the host-task dependency completes. Keep GPU hit and transfer work on their current separate queues and preserve their explicit completion dependencies; do not wait on work queued behind the host-task on the same in-order graph queue, which can deadlock. If callback work must enqueue device work, first route that work through a distinct queue whose dependency and completion are explicit; reject the experiment if its queue ordering cannot be represented without a host wait cycle.

Do not use native graph recording for the initial experiment. The extension document says ordinary `handler::host_task` is unsupported under `enable_native_recording`; only the extension enqueue-functions host-task form is documented for that mode (lines 2208–2213). Use the regular explicit/recorded graph route and runtime capability checks. Also avoid a mutable graph slot while an execution may still be active. The usage guide says a graph is normally prevented from concurrent execution to avoid data races and graph update requires host synchronization (lines 69–76). A single in-flight request with full drain before updating the descriptor is the smallest safe prototype, but limits overlap and may negate any benefit.

## Measurement and acceptance

First capture actual runtime/compiler versions and query graph aspects (`ext_oneapi_limited_graph`, `ext_oneapi_graph`), host-task support and relevant native-recording support for the deployed device. Then run a small correctness fixture on that exact runtime: pre-segment writes sequence/payload; host-task checks and consumes it, writes the next descriptor; dependent post-segment validates it. Include an intentionally failing host-task, asynchronous error propagation, repeated replay with changing descriptors, and verify no slot reuse before completion. Add the production dispatch only after that fixture passes.

For the performance comparison, retain the same serialized handoff policy, model, prompt/output, routes, worker settings and queue topology; compare current segmented path and graph-host-task path in separate clean runs. Record request/window counts and per-window timestamps for graph submission, pre-region completion, host-task entry/exit, copy-queue enqueue/completion, post-region submission/completion, total decode latency and errors. Separate host callback CPU duration from waits and queue submission. Report the critical-path union rather than summing overlapping counters. Keep the first diagnostic short and unprofiled for endpoint latency; use one bounded diagnostic run to attribute phases. Acceptance requires exact output/token and fault-path parity, no concurrent mapped reads, no hangs, and a repeatable reduction in end-to-end decode latency beyond run variation. If total latency is unchanged or worse, retain the safe graph implementation only if it materially simplifies protocol; otherwise keep the current segmented route.

## Decision

This is a reasonable, tightly scoped experiment because the closed receipt has a measurable ~55 ms/window per-layer host service interval and the source exposes the explicit sync/launch boundary. It is not yet a recommended production optimization: the expected host-task graph partitioning may preserve the same boundary costs or add overhead, and deployed-runtime capability/behavior is unverified. The lowest-risk first test is an isolated descriptor handoff fixture, followed by an opt-in one-layer production comparison with complete drain and the unchanged segmented safety policy.
